briefs.summary: Microsoft’s latest quarter shows lower cash-capex free cash flow, while dividends and finance-lease payments remain separate parts of the cash picture.

sections.heading: The quarter
sections.text: Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) generated about $18.63 billion under DFB’s cash-capex free-cash-flow calculation in its fiscal 2027 first quarter, ended September 30, 2026—down about 27% from a year earlier. DFB defines this measure as operating cash flow minus cash additions to property and equipment. The comparison uses reported figures before rounding for presentation.

sections.heading: Dividends and other cash uses
sections.text: Cash dividends paid were about $6.76 billion, or roughly 36% of that measure. This comparison does not account for every competing use of cash: the amount left after dividends is not necessarily available for discretionary spending.

sections.heading: Finance leases
sections.text: Finance-lease principal also sits outside this cash-capex measure. Microsoft separately reported $1.0 billion of financing cash outflows from finance leases. Deducting that principal would produce a different analytical measure; lease interest already included in operating cash flow should not be deducted again.

sections.heading: The next comparison
sections.text: The next quarter will provide another comparison. For now, these figures describe one period—not a forecast of future dividends. Keeping cash capital spending, lease principal and distributions separate makes the change easier to interpret.

briefs.limitations: Cash-capex free cash flow is DFB-defined operating cash flow less cash additions to property and equipment, not an issuer-reported FCF figure. The additional lease-principal deduction is analytical. Derived figures are arithmetic on rounded reported inputs; the dividend remainder excludes other investing and financing cash flows. One quarter does not establish future distribution capacity.

sections.heading: Cash generation
sections.text: Keurig Dr Pepper’s November 3 earnings release details cash generation alongside substantial financing obligations. For the first nine months of 2026, operating cash flow was $2.220 billion. Subtracting $457 million of property, plant and equipment purchases and adding $145 million of disposal proceeds produces KDP’s reported non-GAAP free cash flow of $1.908 billion.

sections.heading: Other financing claims
sections.text: Common cash dividends of $938 million leave a calculated $970 million difference against that free-cash-flow measure. This is before other financing uses, including $107 million of preferred dividends, $64 million of distributions to non-controlling interests and $146 million of finance-lease payments. Excluding property-disposal proceeds, operating cash flow less PP&E purchases was $1.763 billion; this is a separate calculation, not KDP’s defined free cash flow.

sections.heading: Current obligations
sections.text: At September 30, KDP reported $1.290 billion of cash and cash equivalents and $7.270 billion of short-term borrowings and the current portion of long-term obligations. That balance-sheet classification alone does not establish individual repayment dates.

sections.heading: What remains
sections.text: The near-term question is how much cash remains after distributions and other commitments as the company works toward its planned separation. The release supports a cash-coverage observation, not a dividend-safety guarantee.

briefs.limitations: Issuer-defined non-GAAP free cash flow includes PP&E disposal proceeds. The common-dividend difference is not unrestricted or discretionary cash and excludes other investing and financing uses. Operating cash flow less PP&E purchases is a separate analytical measure. Balance-sheet current classification alone is not an individual repayment schedule. Historical cash coverage is not a guarantee or forecast of dividends. The release financial statements are unaudited. Exhibit 99.1 is furnished under Item 2.02, not deemed filed for Section 18; issuer and SEC copies are two official representations of the same company statement, not independent economic corroboration.

sections.heading: Charge and cash
sections.text: 3M’s November 4 filing separates a $7.35 billion nominal settlement commitment from a planned pretax charge of approximately $5.8 billion. The charge, expected in the fourth quarter of 2026, reflects the present value of contributions under its November 3 PFAS personal-injury settlement, rather than an immediate cash payment.

sections.heading: Payment timing
sections.text: An initial $50 million is due within 30 days of the settlement. No payments are scheduled in 2027. The first $1.045 billion main installment is scheduled for January 15, 2028, or 30 days after termination rights are exhausted or waived, whichever is later.

sections.heading: Conditional schedule
sections.text: The six main installments add to $6.27 billion. Including the initial payment and potential additional payments, the schedule’s listed maximum totals $7.35 billion through 2034. Actual amounts and timing depend on participation and other conditions; all payments after the initial one are contingent on neither party exercising termination rights.

sections.heading: What remains
sections.text: 3M says the charge will be treated as a special item in adjusted results and leaves its 2026 guidance unchanged. That accounting treatment does not remove future cash obligations. The question to follow is how settlement participation and conditions translate into actual payments alongside the company’s other commitments.

briefs.limitations: This record describes settlement terms as of November 3, 2026, not a historical operating reporting period. Contractual payment dates extend into the future; the reported charge is approximate present value, not an immediate cash outflow. The schedule lists maximum amounts, with participation, termination and other conditions. The filing was dated November 3 but the SEC index gives a November 4 filing date; no exact public-availability timestamp is claimed. No estimate of dividend coverage or dividend safety is made. The issuer release and SEC filing are official company representations, not independent economic corroboration.
